The line of Shaiva ascetics who built it was well-known and influential, leaving inscriptions at several places; similar monasteries at Surawaya, Kundalpur, Kadwaha and Terahi.

items.note: Bhilsa is the modern representative of ancient Vidisha, which stood across the Betwa 2 miles to the north; name said to derive from a sun temple Bhailasvamin.
Bhilsa a prosperous centre of Jainism and Hinduism whose temples were destroyed; the Bijamandal mosque said to have been a large temple converted into a mosque.
Bhilsa a provincial capital under the Malwa Sultans; under the Mughals a small administrative unit, renamed Alamgirpur by Aurangzeb; passed to the Marathas in the 18th century.
Besnagar (Vessanagar/Vidisha) in the fork of the Betwa and the Bes; a trade centre in the days of the Buddha; under Ashoka and the Shungas a religious centre.
Prosperous until the Gupta age; by the 10th century Bhilsa on the other side of the river had arisen and the older town was almost deserted; site now marked by mounds.
Besnagar finds (Yakshinis, Kubera, Durga, Seven Mothers); Kham Baba pillar with Brahmi inscription of Heliodoros, ambassador of Antialcidas to King Bhagabhadra, styling himself a Bhagavata.
Twenty caves on the eastern face of Udaygiri hill; Cave 1 (Jain) represents the earliest phase of temple architecture with a small shrine and simple porch.
Caves 6 and 7 contain important historical inscriptions of the Gupta period; Cave 13 a Sheshashayi Vishnu.
Udaypur lies 4 miles by metalled road east of Bareth station (Bina-Bhilsa line); also reached from Basoda, about 8 miles by fair weather road.

claim.value: 4 miles E of Bareth Station; about 8 miles from Basoda

items.note: Udaypur (now a small village) was in the medieval period a place of considerable importance, evidenced by Hindu and Mohammedan monuments.
List of principal monuments: Udayeshvara/Nilkanthesvara temple, Bijamandal, Bara-khambi, Pisnari-ka-mandir, Shahi masjid and mahal, Sher Khan mosque.
One of the Sanskrit inscriptions on the temple records that Udayaditya founded a town, built a Shiva temple and excavated a tank, naming them Udayapura, Udayeshvara and Udayasamudra.

claim.value: Udayāditya Paramāra founded Udayapura (town), Udayeśvara (temple), Udayasamudra (tank)

items.note: Ruins of the tank Udayasamudra are seen a short distance north-east of the town.

claim.value: ruins a short distance NE of the town

items.note: Two other inscriptions: construction commenced in V.S. 1116 (A.D. 1059); flag staff erected in V.S. 1137 (A.D. 1080).
Concludes the temple was built by order of Udayaditya Paramara between 1059 and 1080.
Temple stands in a spacious square courtyard with a rectangular projection on each side; dwarf compound wall carved on the outer face; stone seats along the inner face; probably four entrances.
Each entrance a flight of steps with dvarapala figures; only the east one open; the temple was surrounded by eight attendant shrines, at least six with spires.
Attendant shrines in ruin; the shrine in front locally called Vedi (sacrificial hall or Nandi shelter, purpose uncertain); a corresponding one at the back cleared for a mosque.
Principal temple: garbhagriha, sabhamandapa and three praveshamandapas on three sides of the hall, main entrance east; large Siva linga on a high pedestal.
The linga is covered by a brass sheet with a face in relief; its inscription says it was presented by Khande Rao Appaji, a general of Mahadaji Scindia, in V.S. 1841 (A.D. 1775).

claim.key: brass cover of the liṅga: donor
claim.value: Khande Rao Appaji, general of Mahadaji Scindia, V.S. 1841 (1775)

items.note: Pillars and seats in the three porches carry numerous Sanskrit inscriptions, some of historical interest, others merely pilgrim records.
Exterior adorned with Brahma, Vishnu, Ganesha, Kartikeya and the eight Guardians of the Quarters; figures of Shiva and Durga predominate.

Hall and porches have low pyramidal roofs; shrine crowned by a tall shikhara with miniature repetitions and medallions; a human figure near the pinnacle interpreted as the architect or the royal builder.
Temple figure sculptures mutilated by invaders; popular legend blames Aurangzeb, but the text thinks Muhammad Tughlaq earlier did it, building the rear mosque in 1336-38 (two Persian inscriptions).

claim.value: damage popularly attributed to Aurangzeb; text prefers Muhammad Tughlaq (mosque 1336-38)

items.note: Described as a fine example of the Aryavarta style in its fully developed stage, pink sandstone, the spire perhaps unrivalled in beauty; few better examples of medieval northern temple architecture.
Bijamandal or Ghadiyalan-ka-makan: remnant of a two-storeyed house, probably of the temple time-keeper; unfinished Sanskrit inscription opens with praise of the Sun-god.
Bara-khambi: surviving Sabhamandapa of a ruined 11th century temple on the village outskirts; hall with raised seats and a massive slab ceiling.
Pisnari-ka-mandir popularly said to have been built from a woman earnings from grinding flour for the Udayeshvara workmen; the text says its style shows a much later structure.
Shahi Masjid, ruined, locally so called; Persian inscription says begun under Jehangir and completed under Shah-jahan in A.H. 1041 (A.D. 1632).
Remains of a mahal, probably the Mughal-period local governor residence, in early Mughal style with good stone jali work; mosque and graveyard its adjuncts.
Town surrounded by a fortification wall with gates, continued south to a fortified hill; outside the eastern Moti Darwaza stands a small mosque with graveyard.
Mosque in Mandu style with Persian and Sanskrit inscriptions: built by an agent of Sherkhan under Chiyas Shah Khilji of Mandu in A.H. 894 (A.D. 1488).
A big step-well locally called Ghoddaud-ki-baodi, with steps along which horses could run down.
Rock sculptures near Udaypur: unfinished Shiva image locally Ravan tor, and a Sapta Matrika panel on an adjoining hill.
